title: Marriage in 1934 and living on Water Street
summary: He married in 1934 on a tiny wage, lived in one room on Water Street, kept warm with coal from passing trains, and had a landlord complain about his piano practice.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: I got married in 34.
And what were you working at for a living when you got married? At the drugstore. You still working at the drugstore? You got married on the four dollars a week?
On that four dollars a week. I was paying 60 cents a week and couldn't pay that.
60 cents a week?
The landlord come on Saturday for a rent, I'd give him 50 cents. I'd say, I owe you a dime. 50 cents a week?
Where were you living then?
I lived on Water Street.
And the rent was 60 cents a week? Cost of Oakland and Water, yeah.
4033 Water Street. And what kind of a place did you have?
I had one room.

Cooked, eaten, everything else. That one room. Had my clothes in the egg box. Cooked on a grate. Cooked with tar blocks. Train passed by with chocolate with storm cool on. I unloaded in my yard. That's how I kept my family warm.
Oh, you mean they just dropped coal in the yard?
No, the coal. Coal box passed by. I'd get up on that toilet cool over in my yard.
Oh. And then, and how long did you live there at that 60 cents? You paid 50 cents for him?
I stayed there until my first child was born.
And when was that?
Well, he was born, he was born in the last part of March 8, 35, 34.
And then where did you move to?
Moved another hour, two hours a week. Two hours a week?
Oh, that was high rent.
That was room in the kitchen, two hours a week. Wow. Landon put my mind, I made too much noise. What, playing the piano?
Yeah. He didn't like to hear you practice? No.
Me, I'm playing the ball.
